newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan stock bull run ended by central bank, Deng.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan stock bull run ended by central bank, Deng.

text.p: A bull run on Taiwan's stock market ground to a halt on Tuesday after bearish comments from the central bank governor and reports that the health of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping was deteriorating.
But securities analysts said the setback was mild and temporary, and the market would soon resume its surge.
Separately, Taiwan cautioned its businessmen about the potential risk of investing in China after Deng dies.

"It is difficult to predict what would happen (in China) after Deng dies, and businessmen must be cautious in their investment on the mainland," Yiin Chii-ming, vice economics minister, told reporters.

The weighted stock index dropped 162.47 points at the opening on Tuesday, mainly in response to comments late on Monday by central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong, who said the bourse had risen "slightly too much".
However, the market recovered to close only 45.15 points, or 0.59 percent, lower at 7,642.03.
It was only the second time the bourse has finished down in the past 12 trading days. The index has soared nearly 500 points during that span, hitting a six-year peak on Monday.
Analysts said while Sheu's remark prompted many investors to take profits, others who felt sanguine about the index's outlook saw it as an opportunity to enter the market at bargain prices.

"The market at this high level was especially sensitive towards any bearish news, especially for many investors who have seen the values of their shares soar recently," said Lin Long-hsien, securities analyst for United Securities.
"But then other people were willing to buy and support the market when it was down. This shows that the overall sentiment was still quite bullish," Lin added.
In remarks seen to allay concerns aroused by Sheu's comments, Finance Minister Paul Chiu said: "The stock market was moving in a normal direction." He declined to elaborate.

Brokers said the market's ability to stave off a bigger tumble was impressive considering it was hit by reports that Deng's failing health had forced China's leaders to return to Beijing from short trips.
China on Tuesday played down fears over the ailing patriarch, saying there had been no big change in his health.
Brokers said the reports had a mainly psychological impact on investors.
"The rumours on Deng prompted some investors to sell, but the market's small loss indicated that there was no sentiment of panic," said Oliver Fang, senior analyst at National Securities.
But George Hou, a fund manager for Jardine Fleming, said: "It just seemed like not many investors really cared about what was happening to Deng and all the speculation about his health.
"I think unless Deng actually dies, there is not going to be much of a reaction to any rumours," Hou added.
Other analysts said fears that further rumours on Deng could rock the market might prompt Taiwan's government to scrap any effort to curb its growth, thus boosting investor confidence.
Taiwan and China have been diplomatic rivals since a civil war split them in 1949. More than 30,000 Taiwan businessmen have poured an estimated US$25 billion worth of investment in China.
Brokers expect the stock market to hit the 7,800-point level before encountering significant resistance.
The stock market has been buoyed by bullishness on Wall Street and by the widespread expectation that Taiwan is heading for solid economic growth.
The central bank has predicted the island's gross domestic product would grow 6.17 percent in 1997, up from an official forecast of 5.7 percent for 1996.
